title_en: Lu Yongfang v. China Life Insurance Co., Ltd., Taicang Branch — insurance contract dispute
ruling_gist_en: Where a life insurance contract does not stipulate a specific method for premium payment, and the policyholder and the insurer have formed a relatively fixed method of premium payment over a long period, this shall be deemed as the parties having established a specific transaction custom. If the insurance company unilaterally changes the transaction custom in violation of the principle of utmost good faith, causing the policyholder to fail to pay the premium in a timely manner, the policy shall not be deemed invalid on this basis, and the insurance company has no right to suspend the effectiveness of the contract or rescind the insurance contract.

full_text_en:
Lu Yongfang v. China Life Insurance Company Limited, Taicang Branch — insurance contract dispute

Ruling Summary

Where an insurance contract for life insurance does not stipulate a specific method for premium payment, and the policyholder and the insurer have developed a relatively fixed method of premium payment over a long period, it shall be deemed that the parties have established a specific course of dealing. If the insurer unilaterally changes the course of dealing in violation of the principle of utmost good faith, thereby causing the policyholder to fail to pay premiums in a timely manner, the policy shall not be deemed invalid on that basis, and the insurer is not entitled to suspend the effectiveness of the contract or rescind the insurance contract.

Plaintiff: Lu Yongfang, female, 42 years old, residing at Xinbei Street, Shaxi Town, Taicang City.

Defendant: China Life Insurance Company Limited, Taicang Branch, domiciled at Xianfu Street, Chengxiang Town, Taicang City.

Plaintiff Lu Yongfang initiated this lawsuit with the People's Court of Taicang City, Jiangsu Province, due to an insurance contract dispute with Defendant China Life Insurance Company Limited, Taicang Branch (hereinafter referred to as Taicang Life Insurance Company).

Plaintiff Lu Yongfang alleged: Through the contact of insurance agent Liu Ying, Lu Yongfang and Defendant Taicang Life Insurance Company entered into a "Children's Lifetime Happiness Insurance" policy on February 13, 1997, with the insurance period commencing at 12:00 on February 14, 1997, a premium payment period of 15 years, and an annual premium of RMB 720. Taicang Life Insurance Company sent premium payment notices each year, and Lu Yongfang paid the premiums according to the notices. However, starting from 2009, Taicang Life Insurance Company, without reason, ceased sending premium payment notices, causing Lu Yongfang to fail to pay the premiums on time. Subsequently, Lu Yongfang reported the situation to Taicang Life Insurance Company, but Taicang Life Insurance Company refused to accept the premiums on the grounds that the policy had lapsed, leading to a dispute. Therefore, Lu Yongfang filed this lawsuit with the court, requesting judgment: (1) ordering Taicang Life Insurance Company to reinstate the effectiveness of the policy and continue to accept premium payments; (2) ordering Taicang Life Insurance Company to compensate Lu Yongfang for losses of RMB 2,000 incurred in seeking reinstatement of the policy; (3) ordering Taicang Life Insurance Company to bear the litigation costs.

Defendant Taicang Life Insurance Company argued: (1) The Insurance Law stipulates that paying premiums is the obligation of the policyholder; (2) Reminding policyholders to pay premiums is not a statutory obligation of the insurer; (3) The Insurance Law provides that a life insurance contract that has not been paid for more than two years becomes permanently invalid. In this case, the insurance contract had not been paid for more than two years, so the contract had already become invalid. Therefore, the defendant requested the court to reject Lu Yongfang's claims.

The People's Court of Taicang City, Jiangsu Province, found the following facts at first instance:

On February 13, 1997, policyholder Lu Yongfang insured with China Life Insurance Company, Taicang Branch (which changed to Defendant Taicang Life Insurance Company in 2003) a "Children's Lifetime Happiness Insurance" policy for the insured person Dong Haiwei. The insurance period commenced at 12:00 on February 14, 1997, with a premium payment period of 15 years, an annual premium payment method, and a premium of RMB 720. The insurance clauses under "Provisions on Payment, Lapse, and Reinstatement," Article 11, stated: "The premium payment period for annual premium payment shall be the month corresponding to the annual effective date of the insurance policy." Article 12 stated: "The month following the premium payment period shall be the grace period, during which the insurer shall still bear insurance liability. If the premium is still not paid within the grace period, the insurance policy shall automatically lapse, and the insurer shall not bear insurance liability." Article 13 stated: "Within two years after the policy has lapsed, the policyholder and the insured, if they still meet the insurance conditions specified in Article 3 of these clauses, may apply to the insurer for reinstatement. After review and approval by the insurer, the policyholder shall pay the premiums due during the lapse period and interest before the policy can be reinstated." When Lu Yongfang took out the insurance, she directly paid the first year's premium. In the following two years, Liu Ying, an agent of Taicang Life Insurance Company, personally collected the cash premiums from Lu Yongfang at her home each year. Starting from 2000, Taicang Life Insurance Company commissioned the postal department to send premium payment notices to Lu Yongfang. From then until 2008, Lu Yongfang paid the premiums each year at the bank designated by Taicang Life Insurance Company, according to the instructions on the payment notice, and directly obtained premium receipts at the bank. In 2009, Taicang Life Insurance Company again commissioned the postal department to send premium payment notices, but Lu Yongfang claimed she did not receive the notice. After 2010, just before the premium payment period was about to expire, Taicang Life Insurance Company terminated its arrangement with the postal department to send premium payment notices to Lu Yongfang. In May 2011, when Liu Ying asked her sister to visit Lu Yongfang's home to handle bank direct debit for premium payments, Lu Yongfang learned that her failure to pay premiums on time had resulted in the policy lapsing. In the same month, she applied to Taicang Life Insurance Company for policy reinstatement, but Taicang Life Insurance Company refused.

The People's Court of Taicang City, Jiangsu Province, held at first instance:

Plaintiff Lu Yongfang, for the insured Dong Haiwei, purchased personal property insurance from Defendant Taicang Life Insurance Company. Taicang Life Insurance Company issued the policy, and the insurance contract was lawfully established and became effective. According to Article 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (I), "For contracts established before the implementation of the Contract Law, if the performance period stipulated in the contract spans the date of implementation of the Contract Law, or the performance period is after the implementation of the Contract Law, disputes arising from the performance of the contract shall be governed by the relevant provisions of Chapter IV of the Contract Law." Therefore, both Lu Yongfang and Taicang Life Insurance Company should also follow Article 60, paragraph 2, of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, performing their duties in good faith and fulfilling obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality in accordance with the nature, purpose, and course of dealing of the contract. In the insurance clauses concerning payment, lapse, and reinstatement, the policyholder should have paid the annual premium in February of each year. This was an obligation of the policyholder, but the insurance clauses did not specify a specific payment method. According to the testimony of Taicang Life Insurance Company agent Liu Ying and the statements of Taicang Life Insurance Company, the premiums for the second and third years after the contract was concluded were collected by Liu Ying at Lu Yongfang's home. Thereafter, until 2008, the policyholder paid the premiums at the time and place indicated in the premium payment notices sent by Taicang Life Insurance Company through the postal department. The parties had established a specific course of dealing. In 2009, although Taicang Life Insurance Company commissioned the postal department to send premium payment notices, Taicang Life Insurance Company did not provide evidence to prove that the postal department sent the notice to Lu Yongfang as agreed. In 2010, just before the premium payment period was about to expire, Taicang Life Insurance Company no longer sent premium payment notices. Taicang Life Insurance Company unilaterally discontinued its obligation to effectively notify Lu Yongfang, causing Lu Yongfang to fail to pay premiums on time. The restructuring did not change the obligations formed by the course of dealing, including Taicang Life Insurance Company's obligation to collect premiums and provide payment notification. Therefore, the responsibility for the policy lapsing due to the policyholder's failure to pay premiums for two years should be borne by Taicang Life Insurance Company. Taicang Life Insurance Company was not entitled to directly suspend the validity of the contract and rescind the insurance contract based on the provisions of the Insurance Law and the insurance clauses. Accordingly, the court at first instance supported Lu Yongfang's claim that Taicang Life Insurance Company should continue to perform its contractual obligations. Regarding Lu Yongfang's claim for compensation of RMB 2,000 in losses, as Lu Yongfang failed to provide evidence to support this claim, it was not supported.

Based on the foregoing, the People's Court of Taicang City, in accordance with Article 36 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 60, paragraph 2, of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on November 20, 2012:

1. Plaintiff Lu Yongfang and Defendant Taicang Life Insurance Company shall continue to perform the "Children's Lifetime Happiness Insurance Contract" entered into on February 13, 1997;

2. Defendant Taicang Life Insurance Company shall, within 10 days from the effective date of this judgment, accept the premiums payable by Plaintiff Lu Yongfang for 2009 and subsequent years;

3. All other claims of Plaintiff Lu Yongfang are dismissed.

After the first-instance judgment, Taicang Life Insurance Company, dissatisfied, appealed to the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court, arguing: (1) The first-instance court erred in its findings. First, the first-instance judgment characterized the insurer's right to collect premiums as an obligation, confusing the concepts of the insurer's rights and obligations. Second, according to Article 58 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China (1995), the reinstatement of the contract's validity is not an obligation of the insurer but a matter to be agreed upon by both parties through negotiation. (2) The first-instance court incorrectly applied the law. First, according to the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, paying premiums is a statutory obligation of the policyholder. Regardless of whether the insurance company fulfills its notification obligation, the policyholder must fulfill the obligation to pay premiums. Moreover, the policyholder had paid premiums for 12 years and should have clearly known the payment time. The policyholder's failure to pay based solely on not receiving a payment notice should result in the corresponding legal consequences. Second, the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China is a general law, while the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China is a special law. According to legal principles, the special law prevails over the general law. The first-instance judgment's use of the general law to override the special law was an incorrect application of the law. In summary, the appellant requested the second-instance court to set aside the first-instance judgment and render a new judgment.

The appellee, Lu Yongfang, responded: (1) When purchasing insurance, Lu Yongfang, as an ordinary person, could not accurately understand whether the content of the insurance contract was fair and just, nor could she genuinely understand the meaning of the clauses and relevant legal provisions at the time of signing the contract. (2) In the early stages of the contract performance, the appellant Taicang Life Insurance Company's agents collected premiums at Lu Yongfang's home. Later, Lu Yongfang paid premiums at the bank based on premium payment notices. After paying premiums for 12 years, just before the payment period was about to expire, Taicang Life Insurance Company, in violation of good faith, unilaterally stopped sending payment notices without Lu Yongfang's knowledge. (3) In fact, Lu Yongfang did not refuse to pay premiums; rather, the insurance company sought to render the contract invalid, with the underlying intention of evading its claim settlement obligations. Therefore, the liability for failing to pay premiums rests entirely with Taicang Life Insurance Company. In summary, the appellee requested the appeal be dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

The Suzhou Intermediate People's Court, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Suzhou Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province held at second instance:

Article 60 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides that parties shall fully perform their obligations as agreed. Parties shall adhere to the principle of good faith and fulfill obligations of notification, assistance, and confidentiality in accordance with the nature, purpose, and course of dealing of the contract. Based on the facts as found, in the first two years of performance of the insurance contract in question, the appellant Taicang Life Insurance Company's agent collected premiums from the appellee Lu Yongfang at her home. Starting in 2000, Taicang Life Insurance Company commissioned the postal department to send premium payment notices to Lu Yongfang. From then until 2008, Lu Yongfang paid premiums each year at the bank designated by Taicang Life Insurance Company according to the instructions on the payment notice. Accordingly, first, the parties had established a certain course of dealing regarding premium payment, namely, Taicang Life Insurance Company either collected premiums at Lu Yongfang's home or notified the policyholder to pay premiums at a designated location. Moreover, during the performance of the contract, Taicang Life Insurance Company had requested the policyholder to change the premium payment method (i.e., from home collection in the first two years to payment at a designated bank according to a payment notice). Under such circumstances, the policyholder could not be sure whether the annual payment method was the same. Therefore, as the insurer, Taicang Life Insurance Company was even more obligated to notify the policyholder each year of the premium payment and the method of payment. However, during the performance of the insurance contract in question, Taicang Life Insurance Company had no evidence to prove that it delivered the premium payment notice to the policyholder Lu Yongfang in 2009, and after 2010, it did not send any premium payment notice to Lu Yongfang. Based on the foregoing analysis, it is clear that the primary responsibility for the policyholder Lu Yongfang's failure to pay premiums for two years lies with the insurer, Taicang Life Insurance Company. Under these circumstances, Taicang Life Insurance Company is not entitled to suspend the validity of the contract or claim rescission of the contract solely based on the relevant provisions of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China and the relevant terms of the contract. Where special laws provide clear provisions, special laws shall prevail. Where special laws do not provide clear provisions, the relevant provisions of general laws shall apply. Therefore, the first-instance court's application of the relevant provisions of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, in the absence of clear provisions in the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, was lawful and well-founded. Taicang Life Insurance Company's appeal argument that the first-instance court incorrectly applied the law is manifestly untenable.

In conclusion, the facts found in the first-instance judgment are clear, the application of the law is correct, and the substantive disposition is proper. In accordance with Article 170, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on January 18, 2013:

Appeal dismissed; original judgment affirmed.

This judgment is final.
